interest: This file uniquely illuminates the transnational reach of Japan's agrarian reform, illustrating how domestic land redistribution collided with international law and property rights of overseas emigrants and dual citizens across North and Latin America. It offers valuable insight into the mechanics of serving compulsory purchase writs through Japanese-American newspapers, alongside rich empirical data from an extensive 1949 rural survey capturing grassroots peasant attitudes toward tenancy, cooperatives, and reform.
keywords: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP)
Japanese Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry
overview: This file comprehensively documents the legislative enactment, administrative implementation, and international ramifications of Japan's postwar agrarian land reform under the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP) between 1946 and 1949. It brings together full statutory texts, translations, and imperial ordinances—notably the Agricultural Land Adjustment Law and the Owner-Farmer Establishment Special Measures Law—alongside Ministry of Agriculture handbooks and Diet commentaries. A significant portion of the file details the diplomatic, legal, and administrative challenges of expropriating agricultural lands owned by absentee landlords abroad, foreign nationals, and dual Japanese-American citizens across North and Latin America, including hundreds of individual purchase writs served via diaspora newspapers. Additionally, the collection features SCAP directives enforcing reform against landlord resistance, policy correspondence regarding Allied and foreign property rights, and an extensive GHQ sociological field survey evaluating rural tenant and farmer attitudes toward the reforms.
